messages.subject: CI of population estimate
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA-team,
I hope you can give me some directions for the following problem. I am fitting a rw2d model to porpoise counts on a regular 10x10 km grid. The porpoises have been counted along transects and so there are quite some gridcells with no observations. For those gridcells with observations, I include the surveyed area as an offset.

formula = count ~ f(node, model="rw2d", nrow=nrow, ncol=ncol)
offsetter = log(gr$area)
data = data.frame(count=gr$count,offsetter=log(gr$area),node=node)
result=inla(formula, family="poisson", offset=offsetter, data=data)
q <- exp(result$summary.fixed[1] + result$summary.random$node$mean)

Summing the q gives a population estimate that is pretty similar to the population estimate based on conventional distance sampling methods (Buckland et al 2001). Very nice!

But now, I would like to estimate the 95% CI around this population estimate. I have tried various things, such as taking the 95% bounds of the intercept, but all give unrealistic outcomes. SD values of the node go up to 20; the SD of the intercept is 2.03. Moreover, I have tried various settings of prior.spat, and above a certain level (30), the SDs suddently get very small, but then the smoother doesn't show any detail anymore.

Can you give me any guidance in how to do this or where to find a similar analysis worked out?

Many thanks in advance!

Rob

messages.body_plain:
On 05/11/13 11:54, Rob van Bemmelen wrote:
> result=inla(formula, family="poisson", offset=offsetter, data=data)
> q <- exp(result$summary.fixed[1] + result$summary.random$node$mean)
>
> Summing the q gives a population estimate that is pretty similar to the
> population estimate based on conventional distance sampling methods
> (Buckland et al 2001). Very nice!
>
> But now, I would like to estimate the 95% CI around this population
> estimate. I have tried various things, such as taking the 95% bounds of
> the intercept, but all give unrealistic outcomes.

You'll need to use the information in the posterior distributions as
much as possible to get sensible results.  For point-wise population
density estimates, you can let inla compute the intervals for
exp(intercept+spatial) explicitly.
You just need to add the prediction locations to the model, with "NA" as
data for each of them, set control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE,link=1),
and then extract the results from result$summary.fitted.values.

For the total population, inla cannot calculate the answer exactly due
to the nonlinearity. Lower and upper bounds can be obtained by summing
the lower and upper point-wise bounds.  For tighter bounds, simulation
using inla.posterior.sample() can be used.

I suspect the wide results you got are due to strong posterior
dependences between the latent variables in the model.

PS. Note that all the resulting intervals will be "Bayesian posterior
prediction intervals", which has a slightly different technical
interpretation compared with a "frequentist confidence interval".

Finn L

messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA experts:

I hope to make inference of the following model with INLA:

The hidden process model is a random walk, which is of our main interest:

X[t]  = X[t-1] + epsilon[t], epsilon[t] iid N(0, tao_0), for t=1, 2,...T

and we have two sources of observations of this random walk:

The first one is an systematically biased observation of it

Y[t] = a + b*X[t] + xi[t], xi[t]  iid N(0, tao_1), for t=1, 2,...T

and another set of unbiased observations, but we only have them at a small subset of time points:

Y*[t] = X[t] + zeta[t], zeta[t] iid N(0, tao_2), for t in tSubset={1, 5, 20, 50, ....}

I read through the examples in ``Tools to manipulate models and likelihoods" and believe INLA should be able to deal with this problem, but I do not know how to

1. How to specify two different normal likelihoods for two sets of observations of unequal length.
2. How to make the linear combination (matrix A) of the random effects only apply to a subset of observations.
3. Is it possible to make inference of the elements in A (parameter b in the second equation in my description) ?

Thank you very much.

Seagle

>
> this gives an spde model with no parameters, and the given values for

Simply expand the B-matrices into column matrices:

spde=inla.spde2.matern(mesh,
   B.tau=matrix(log(tau), mesh$n, 1),
   B.kappa=matrix(log(kappa), mesh$n, 1))

If tau and kappa are vectors of length mesh$m that should give you what
you ask for.

messages.subject: Scaling IGMRF priors
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA team,

we are very interested in scaling IGMRF priors. We are trying to understand how INLA scales models by means of the “scale.model=T” option. We built the code reported below for a binomial-logit model with a RW2 prior on temporal random effects. We estimated 4 models:

Model 1: use the INLA “RW2” prior, the model is not scaled

Model 2: use the INLA “generic0” model with precision matrix Kt, the model is not scaled

Results obtained by means of these two models are absolutely comparable

Model 1.1: use the INLA “RW2” prior, the model IS scaled

Model 2.1: use the INLA “generic0” model with precision matrix “scaled.Kt” obtained as Kt*gv(Kt)^2 (the generalised variance)

Results obtained by means of these two models are quite different. We built Model 2.1 trying to reproduce the same model scaling performed by INLA but looks like we are wrong.

We need to manage this issue by means of the “generic0” model since we need to scale priors for latent models with different structures with respect to those included in INLA. Do you have some suggestion?
Thanks
Fedele and Carlo

library(spam)
library(INLA)
library(MASS)

###COMPUTES THE GENERALISED STANDARD DEVIATION (SORBYE and RUE, 2013)
gv<-function(x) exp(mean(.5*log(diag(ginv(as.matrix(x))))))

##DATA SIMULATION
TT<-100
trials<-10
means<-rnorm(TT*trials,rep(seq(-1.96,1.96,l=TT),each=trials),.4)
y<-rbinom(length(means),trials,pnorm(means))

##PRECISION MATRIX and DATA
Kt<-precmat.RW2(TT)
tt<-rep(1:TT,each=trials)
dat<-data.frame(y=y,tt=tt)

###MODEL 1 INLA RW2 prior
formula1<- y ~  -1 + f(tt, model="rw2", scale.model=F, constr=F)
mod1<-inla(formula1, data = dat, family="binomial", Ntrials=rep(trials,TT), control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE))

###MODEL 2 RW2 prior built by model="generic0"
formula2<- y ~  -1 + f(tt, model="generic0", Cmatrix=as.matrix(Kt), rankdef=2, constr=F)
mod2<-inla(formula2, data = dat, family="binomial", Ntrials=rep(trials,TT), control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE))

mod1$summary.hyper
mod2$summary.hyper

####SCALED MODELS
###MODEL 1.1 INLA RW2 prior - scaled model
formula1.1<- y ~  -1 + f(tt, model="rw2", scale.model=T, constr=F)
mod1.1<-inla(formula1.1, data = dat, family="binomial", Ntrials=rep(trials,TT), control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE))

###MODEL 2 RW2 prior built by model="generic0" - scaled model?
scaled.Kt<-Kt*gv(Kt)^2
formula2.1<- y ~  -1 + f(tt, model="generic0", Cmatrix=as.matrix(scaled.Kt), rankdef=2, constr=F)
mod2.1<-inla(formula2.1, data = dat, family="binomial", Ntrials=rep(trials,TT), control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE))

mod1.1$summary.hyper
mod2.1$summary.hyper

Thanks for your email with good questions.

There are two issues. First, is that the default prior for the rw2 and
generic model is different, so doing

formula1.1<- y ~  -1 +

  f(tt, model="rw2", scale.model=T, constr=F,
    hyper = list(prec = list(param = c(1, 0.001))))

formula2.1<- y ~  -1 + f(tt, model="generic0",
Cmatrix=as.matrix(scaled.Kt),

rankdef=2, constr=F,
 hyper = list(prec = list(param = c(1, 0.001))))

which ensure that the prior is the same, gives

> mod1.1$summary.hyper[,"mean"]
[1] 919.5912716
> mod2.1$summary.hyper[,"mean"]
[1] 920.0041533

which is almost the same.

The reason for this difference again, is twofold. First, we do not do

gv<-function(x) exp(mean(.5*log(diag(ginv(as.matrix(x))))))

but we scale the first and last element of log(diag()) with 0.5 and you
need to divide by 99 instead of doing the 'mean'. this because we want
to integrate the margianal (log) variances between 1 to 100 in this
case.

doing this, gives these scalings:
> gv(Kt)
[1] 41.39025708
> exp(0.5*sum(c(0.5*d[c(1,100)],d[2:99]))/99)
[1] 41.0446375

Secondly, we do not compute 'ginv' as it as to expensive, we use the
'conditioning by Kriging' approach, which preserve the sparsity, so that
the costly ginv() is avoided.

> mod1.1$logfile[grep("scale.model",mod1.1$logfile)]
[1] "                scale.model[1]"
[2] "                scale.model: prec_scale[1678.49]"

so this is

> sqrt(1678.49)
[1] 40.96937881

compared to the numbers above. since this alternative computation is
affected by a 'small epsilon', which is unavoidable.

Hope this helps,

H

> generic model is different, so doing
>
> formula1.1<- y ~  -1 +
>   f(tt, model="rw2", scale.model=T, constr=F,
>     hyper = list(prec = list(param = c(1, 0.001))))
>
> formula2.1<- y ~  -1 + f(tt, model="generic0",
> Cmatrix=as.matrix(scaled.Kt),
> rankdef=2, constr=F,
>  hyper = list(prec = list(param = c(1, 0.001))))
>
> which ensure that the prior is the same, gives
>
> > mod1.1$summary.hyper[,"mean"]
> [1] 919.5912716
> > mod2.1$summary.hyper[,"mean"]
> [1] 920.0041533
>
>
> which is almost the same.
>
> The reason for this difference again, is twofold. First, we do not do
>
> gv<-function(x) exp(mean(.5*log(diag(ginv(as.matrix(x))))))
>
> but we scale the first and last element of log(diag()) with 0.5 and you
> need to divide by 99 instead of doing the 'mean'. this because we want
> to integrate the margianal (log) variances between 1 to 100 in this
> case.
>
> doing this, gives these scalings:
> > gv(Kt)
> [1] 41.39025708
> > exp(0.5*sum(c(0.5*d[c(1,100)],d[2:99]))/99)
> [1] 41.0446375
>
>
> Secondly, we do not compute 'ginv' as it as to expensive, we use the
> 'conditioning by Kriging' approach, which preserve the sparsity, so that
> the costly ginv() is avoided.
>
>
> > mod1.1$logfile[grep("scale.model",mod1.1$logfile)]
> [1] "                scale.model[1]"
> [2] "                scale.model: prec_scale[1678.49]"
>
> so this is
>
> > sqrt(1678.49)
> [1] 40.96937881
>
> compared to the numbers above. since this alternative computation is
> affected by a 'small epsilon', which is unavoidable.

The full posterior correlation is a large dense matrix, so that can typically not be obtained in practice.

For a smaller number of count and and count2 combinations, you can use the "lincomb" features (see the FAQ), which allows computing the posterior correlation between linear combinations of latent variables.

Another option is to use sample from the posterior to calculate a Monte Carlo estimate of the correlations. (See recent discussion reads in the discussion groups for more information about using inla to sample from the posterior)

Finn

messages.body_plain:
There are a few problems here, mostly to do with the interpretation of the formulas.

- The first big problem is that inla.qinv *does not* compute the inverse of Q!  (Q is a large sparse matrix - you never want to compute its actual inverse, that would be too computationally expensive).  For the record, inla.qinv(Q) computes enough elements of Q^{-1} to compute the Fisher score function (which turns out to be the elements of Q^{-1} correpsonding the non-zero elements of Q).

- The second big problem is that in the formula for the posterior mean, mu is the prior mean and *not* a sample from the prior.  The correct code would be
      mupost = mu + inla.qsolve(Qx+A5TQeps%*%A5, ASTQesp%*%(y- A5%*%mu)
where  mu is the mean of the prior (which is zero).  Note that inla.qsolve is the function (rather than inla.qinv) that you need here.

- The third problem, which is less big, is that even if this was computed correctly, it would not be the same as res5$summary.random$i$mean.  The thing calculated above is the mean of the latent field computed using the plug-in estimates of the hyperparamters (computed as their posterior expectation), whereas the result from the inla call is the mean of the marginal distribution computed by marginalising out the hyperparameters.  These are mathematically different quantities.

I hope this helps.

D

messages.body_plain:
A basic rule in computation is that you almost never need to compute an actual matrix inverse.  With inla.qsolve(Q,b) we solve the linear system Qx=b, which is all that is needed in this situation.  It would be completely infeasible in most cases to compute the full inverse.

So my main suggestion for computing the full inverse is to check if you really really need it.  (And really almost always you don't - you only need to solve a linear system or you need a few elements of the inverse [see q.inv])

If you do, solve(as.matrix(Q)) will do the job, but it will be insanely expensive in terms of time and memory. In this case, I strongly suggest moving to an inference method that *doesn't* require the inverse of a large matrix.

For maximum likelihood estimates, you don't need the full inverse.

Best wishes,

Dan.

(Q is a large sparse matrix - you never want to compute its actual inverse, that would be too computationally expensive).  For the record, inla.qinv(Q) computes enough elements of Q^{-1} to compute the Fisher score function (which turns out to be the elements of Q^{-1} correpsonding the non-zero elements of Q).

> >
> > - The third problem, which is less big, is that even if this was computed correctly, it would not be the same as res5$summary.random$i$mean.  The thing calculated above is the mean of the latent field computed using the plug-in estimates of the hyperparamters (computed as their posterior expectation), whereas the result from the inla call is the mean of the marginal distribution computed by marginalising out the hyperparameters. Hi help!

I am running the spde model with a larger data set which has about  81809 observations. The mesh I generated has 10211 triangles and n.spde = 5247. I also want to predict this on other 81809 locations..

I saw Finn said that he tried even larger data set with a lot of memory .. I wonder if that is the issue of memory ? how can I deal with this? Thanks a lot!

Best,
Xiao

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] inla memory issue?
messages.body_plain:
Using metres as unit for regions of multikilometre regions usually leads to numerical issues.  It's typically more robust to use km as the spatial unit instead, and the defaults in inla are adapted to data and effects on the size order "1". In any case, you need to be careful when constructing the mesh, so that e.g. max.edge is specified in the correct units.  Rescaling space is simply a change of units, and the apart from the relation to the scale of the prior distributions it should have no effect othe results, when interpreted in the correct units.  1000 metres is always 1 km.

Finn

messages.subject_clean: Submit a job to a remote server
messages.body_plain:
We have added an extention of the inla(...,inla.call="remote")  option
which allow for the computations to take place at a remote server.

For a large(r) job, it was unconvenient to keep the connection alive
while waiting for the job to finish, so we have added the option

r = inla(..., inla.call="submit")

so you get your prompt in R back so you can keep working, while the
computations are done at your server. You can check the status of you
job(s) with inla.qstat() and when your job(s) is/are done, they will be
stored at the server and you can retrieve the results later using
r=inla.qget(r). See ?inla.q  for further options. The FAQ entry about
'remote' on www.r-inla.org <http://www.r-inla.org> is updated to reflect these new options.

Best
